The rain fell in steady sheets across the slate roofs, pooling in the gutters and spilling onto the narrow lanes below in thin silver threads. Elena kept her head down and her satchel close, the weight of the wrapped fragment inside it a constant reminder of why she had crossed half the city after dark. The archive doors were unlocked, as Harlan had promised. He sat at the long table beneath the single hanging lamp, tea gone cold, spectacles reflecting the flame. When she set the parchment between them he did not speak at once. He only leaned forward, breath careful, and watched the faded ink catch the light.

They worked through the night. The verses were incomplete, yet the gaps themselves seemed deliberate, spaces left for the reader to step into. One line described a hill where the wind carried voices that had never been spoken aloud. Another mentioned a stone that remembered every hand that had touched it. By dawn they had a rough sequence of landmarks. Harlan packed bread, a flask, and the oldest map he owned. Elena added a spare notebook and the fragment itself, sealed again in oilcloth. They left before the city fully woke.

The road beyond the walls was little more than a track softened by days of rain. Mud sucked at their boots. Brambles snagged sleeves. Twice they lost the path and had to retrace their steps by the angle of a particular ridge the poem had named. Harlan moved slowly, favoring one knee, yet he never suggested turning back. Elena matched his pace and listened to the way he muttered half-lines under his breath, testing them against the landscape as if the land might answer. In the late afternoon they reached a stand of beeches whose trunks were scarred with old carvings. One carving matched a symbol from the fragment exactly. Harlan traced it with a fingertip and nodded once.

They camped beneath those trees. The rain eased to a mist. Elena woke once in the dark and saw Harlan still sitting upright, the map spread across his knees, lamplight low. He was not reading the map. He was staring past it into the trees as though something there had just spoken his name. In the morning he said nothing about it. They walked on.

The clearing appeared without warning. One moment the undergrowth pressed close; the next it opened onto grass so even it looked tended. At the center rose an oak whose lowest branches had grown into loops and angles that echoed the script on the parchment. A door, child-sized and dark with age, was set into the trunk. No hinge showed. Elena knelt and pressed her palm to the wood. It was warm. Harlan crouched beside her, joints protesting. For a long moment neither moved. Then Elena turned the iron ring that served as a handle and the door swung inward on silent hinges.

What lay beyond was not the hollow of a tree. Shelves rose in every direction, built from living wood that still showed green at the cut edges. Books stood spine-out, their covers made of pressed leaves, bark, and something that felt like softened stone. When Elena drew one free, the pages stirred as if a breeze had found them. Words formed and dissolved under her eyes, never quite settling into a single language she knew, yet the sense of them arrived clearly: a memory of a kitchen at dusk, flour on a wooden table, a child’s laugh just out of sight. She closed the book and the memory faded, leaving only the faint scent of yeast.

Harlan had already moved deeper. His voice came back thin with distance. “They are not all memories. Some are possibilities. Look.” He held up a slim volume whose pages showed a street Elena recognized, except the lamps burned blue and the people walking it wore clothes cut in a style she had never seen. When he shut the book the image vanished. They spent hours moving between shelves, opening volumes at random. One contained the precise sound of rain on a particular roof in a city that no longer existed. Another held the weight of a decision never made, the quiet relief and the quieter regret braided together so tightly they could not be separated. A third simply repeated, page after page, the same short sentence in a hand that changed with every line: I was here.

They did not notice the light changing until the shelves nearest the door began to dim. Elena checked the fragment again. A later verse, one they had only half-deciphered, spoke of a toll. Nothing taken by force, the line suggested, but something offered freely if the visitor wished to leave with more than they had brought. Harlan sat on a low root that served as a bench and rubbed his knee. “I have spent forty years cataloguing what other people remembered,” he said. “I am not certain I have many unused hours left to trade.” Elena did not answer at once. She walked a little farther and found a narrow alcove where a single empty shelf waited, its wood pale and unmarked. On the shelf lay a fresh notebook, pages blank, binding still supple. Beside it rested a pen whose nib had never touched ink.

She understood then that the library did not hoard. It exchanged. A reader could carry a story out, but only by leaving a story behind—one that had not yet been written, one that belonged to no one else. The fragment in her satchel was itself such an offering, incomplete until someone chose to finish it. She returned to Harlan and told him what she had seen. He listened, then smiled with the corner of his mouth. “Then we each leave something,” he said. “And we each take something small enough to carry without bending under it.”

They worked until the light outside the door had gone gray. Harlan wrote, in his careful archivist’s hand, the account of a morning forty years earlier when he had first unlocked the archive and found a single window open, rain blowing in across a table of uncatalogued letters. He had closed the window and dried the letters one by one. He had never told anyone. Elena wrote the walk they had just finished, the mud, the carved beech, the moment the door opened, and the precise temperature of the wood under her palm. She left the last page blank on purpose. When they set the two notebooks on the empty shelf the wood darkened slightly, as if accepting moisture. In return each of them chose one slim volume no thicker than a finger. Harlan’s contained the sound of his own name spoken by a voice he had forgotten. Elena’s held a single clear image: the archive table at dawn, tea still warm, and the fragment lying between them exactly as it had that first night, except the missing lines were no longer missing. They did not open the books again until they were outside.

The door closed behind them without a sound. The oak looked ordinary. Rain had started once more, lighter now. They walked back along the track in silence for a long while. At the beech trees Harlan paused and rested a hand on the carved trunk. “We will have to decide what to tell them,” he said. Elena nodded. The satchel felt lighter, though she knew the weight had only changed its nature. Somewhere ahead the city lamps were already being lit. They would reach the archive before full dark if they kept a steady pace. She adjusted the strap on her shoulder and matched her steps to his, the notebook in her coat pocket warm against her ribs, its unread pages waiting for whatever morning would bring.
